headline: Legal industry adopting Chinese open-source AI models, rebranded for Western markets, to capture better margins versus paying OpenAI, Anthropic or Meta
reasoning: Monfort observes that major legal-industry AI players are taking Chinese open-source models, renaming them for Western markets, and using them because the margin profile is superior to licensing from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Meta. He sees this as a meaningful structural dynamic in where AI technology is actually deployed commercially, suggesting the world is more connected than trade-war narratives imply.
quote: I think it is interesting when you see some of the biggest names in the AI space in say, the legal industry, like I'm in taking Chinese open source models, renaming them for Western markets and using those open source models because they get to have better margins than having to pay to open AI, Anthropic, the likes of Meta, etc. So I think that there's a very interesting play there when it comes to where the technology sits. The world is much more connected and we shouldn't be so against all of those things.
episode_title: Why boring may be best when it comes to ETFs

headline: New diversified balanced, growth and high-growth ETFs launched alongside credit income, global semiconductors (Van Eck), rare earth X-China, Quantum, and Blackstone-partnered senior loan and high income products — 11 launches, zero closures
reasoning: Monfort highlights a broad wave of new ETF launches covering diversified balanced (DVBA), diversified growth, and high-growth strategies, plus a credit income fund. Van Eck released global semiconductor and rare earth/strategic metals ex-China ETFs. A Quantum computing ETF was noted as an underappreciated theme despite significant Australian government spending in the space. State Street partnered with Blackstone to launch a senior loan ETF and a high income ETF, as well as an Australian floating rate bond index, giving SMSF and retail investors a wide range of new positioning tools.
quote: The interesting thing is that there were 11, there were no closures. So we track opens and closures. The 11 new ones were across a a diversified range. One of the biggest ones was DVBA, which is a diversified balanced ETF and a diversified growth ETF and high growth ones. So there's also one for credit income. And then on Thematix Van Eck released a few so global semiconductors, another one called resin for rare earth and strategic metals X China. So if you wanted that X this exposure and one for Quantum, which is a play that I hear all about blockchain and digital assets, I hear all about AI. We haven't heard as much about Quantum, even though the Australian government spent billions of dollars trying to get a big Quantum company to come back. And then really interesting, there's some income plays that have come out of State St partnering with Blackstone. So there's a senior loan and a high income ETF that have come out. And then finally an Australian floating rate bond index. So there's some really interesting plays there depending on how people want to position in their portfolios for SMSFS, retail investors and the like.

headline: Bitcoin and Ethereum spot ETFs seeing strong returns driven by US Clarity Act optimism and interest rate sensitivity (risk-on bid)
reasoning: Crypto ETFs, specifically Bitcoin and Ethereum spot products listed on market, were among the top returners in the period. Monfort attributes gains to positive sentiment around the US Clarity Act's wording providing regulatory clarity, plus the same interest rate sensitivity dynamic that is hurting long-duration bonds — a risk-on effect benefiting crypto. Algorithmic traders scanning for positive regulatory signals amplified the move.
quote: The interesting thing there is that they're looking at some implications from the US with some more positive feedback in terms of the Clarity Act anytime there is just like the normal traditional kind of markets crypto investors in the algorithms that are trading that are looking for all of those positive sorts of statements. So the US Clarity Act seeing some positive gains there in terms of the wording, it's that kind of stuff as well as interest rate sensitivity as well. So the opposite effect of what's going on in the bond markets where we're seeing people pulling out a long duration type things where we're seeing that have a positive effect on anything that has risk on and crypto is one of those things.

headline: Australian financials and property underperformed in August but historical pattern shows cyclical rotation — zoom out and the story looks different
reasoning: Monfort observes that Australian financials and property ETFs did not perform well in August, but contextualises this as part of a recurring cyclical pattern where these sectors have months of outperformance followed by months of weakness. headline: Record August ETF inflows of $6.7B dominated by broad-based index funds (A200, STW), not thematics, despite higher returns in copper, gold and crypto
reasoning: Despite 11 new ETF listings on the ASX in August and strong returns in copper, gold, silver and crypto, the bulk of ETF inflows continued to flow into broad-based index funds such as the A200 and STW. Mark Monfort notes this reflects the hub-and-satellite model favoured by SMSFs and retail investors doing dollar cost averaging. August was a record month for inflows at $6.7 billion, the highest since July 2024, though still below the COVID-era highs of late 2020. The contrast between where returns were and where the money went was striking.
quote: The flows have been you would think into the thematics and the trends because that's what a lot of ETF providers have been showing us. There's always a new ETS, we've got 11 new on the board in August on the ASX, but all the money is still going into the broad based index funds. So that's the A2 hundreds STWS, all of those normal names that are in the satellites and hub kind of model where those hubs are being bought up by the various like SMSFS or retailers, you know retail investors doing dollar cost averaging etcetera. But in terms of the the money where the returns were, it wasn't there. It was copper, it was gold, it was even crypto. So it was really interesting to see the contrast between where the money was and where the returns were.

headline: AI doom-and-gloom warnings should be taken with a grain of salt; real gains sit somewhere between hype and panic, but a cost problem still needs solving
reasoning: Mark Monfort argues that Western AI leaders calling for a pause are doing so while China continues full speed ahead, making a slowdown on one side resemble an arms race disadvantage. He notes that much AI cost has been subsidised by VC capital, meaning true costs haven't yet been properly measured. He believes the market sits somewhere between doom-and-gloom and overhype, and that real-world AI adoption is still lower than commonly assumed. He does not see current warnings as panic stations.
quote: I think it's very interesting whenever you see Western leaders in the AI space saying that we need to have a pause because others in other countries, China, etcetera do not have that sort of thing. There is no slow down there. So as soon as you slow down in one side, almost like an arms race like some investors might remember from the 80s, there is just, we should just not slow down. You've got to take a lot of this AI stuff. And I'll put my Foundry Labs hat on because a lot of the stuff we built with ETF tracker, a lot of the stuff I do day to day with my law firm, Madison Marcus is all AI driven. And when it comes to the things that are true there, it is all a grain of salt because some things are doom and gloom and then others are saying that it's all over hype. And when you balance it out and sit somewhere in the middle, you actually see where the real gains are. There is a cost problem that needs to be figured out.
